entry.title: vibeOS and the Speed of AI

link.title: vibeOS and the Speed of AI

entry.content:
Recently I came across VibeOS when I was wasting time scrolling Xiaohongshu. It is an operating system hallucinated with Claude Code. It is not like vibe-coding a frontend, a backend, or something that still follows familiar software development patterns. Here, almost everything feels like hallucination. The LLM is pretending to be an operating system and playing with users. It means every time you open the same page, you may get a different view, thanks to today’s LLM’s next token prediction essence. There are also some funny and slightly chaotic reports around similar vibe-coded OS projects, like the ones from Tom’s Hardware and PC Gamer.

VibeOS desktop screenshot from the VibeOS GitHub repository

What surprised me was the feeling of time collapsing.

Two years ago, when I was grinding ECE391 in Champaign’s brutal winter, operating systems felt almost sacred to me. You had to understand memory, interrupts, scheduling, filesystems, devices, and a hundred small details that punish you when you pretend to understand them. Looking back from today, some of that workflow feels almost primitive: reading docs, using GDB to debug, staring at weird crashes, building things slowly by hand.

A VibeOS browser screenshot from the project repository

Maybe the point is not whether it is a good OS right now. Maybe the point is that an OS can start to become less like a fixed machine and more like a generated world. Maybe one day people will be kept like factory-farmed chickens, each lying inside a coffin-like pod, tubes feeding the mouth and nose, sensors pressed against the forehead, while AI hallucinates a grand, colorful, dramatic life directly into the mind. Software no longer as a tool we operate, but as an environment that operates on us.

entry.title: Thoughts on Suno AI v5 and the Future of Music Creation

link.title: Thoughts on Suno AI v5 and the Future of Music Creation

entry.content:
I was shocked by the recently released Suno AI v5.0 model. As a guitar enthusiast and indie music lover, I was blown away by the quality of music this generation of AI can produce.

Suno AI v5.0: A new era in music generation

Just a year ago, artists were loudly proclaiming that AI could never replace art or music. In just one year, those voices have gone quiet.

The Silver Lining

Looking at the bright side, AI has dramatically lowered the barrier to entry for creative work. It liberates people from the technical constraints, putting human expression at the center and preventing the “toolification” of creators. AI will likely disrupt commercial art, but it won’t kill art itself. In fact, AI development will benefit ordinary creators and music enthusiasts who previously lacked the resources or technical skills to bring their ideas to life.

That said, for those hoping to make a living solely from songwriting, the current pace of development makes that path increasingly challenging.

A Historical Parallel

When photography was invented centuries ago, painters felt similarly threatened. After all, no brushstroke, no matter how refined, could match the precision of a camera. But what did artists do? They pivoted toward the abstract, the expressive, and the purely artistic. They discovered creative paths that cameras couldn’t replicate—giving birth to Cubism, Impressionism, Fauvism, and Pop Art.

Picasso's abstract art: An artistic response to photography that explored new dimensions of expression

I believe music will follow a similar trajectory. Professional musicians will likely move toward purer, more experimental forms of expression. The democratization of music creation might push them to explore territories that AI cannot easily replicate.

Final Thoughts

Rather than fearing AI, perhaps we should view it as a catalyst for artistic evolution. Just as photography didn’t kill painting but rather redefined it, AI music generation won’t kill music either. The future might belong to those who can blend human creativity with AI capabilities, or those who dare to venture into artistic territories that machines cannot comprehend.

As for me? I’ll continue strumming my guitar…
entry.summary: Reflections on AI-generated music and what it means for artists and music lovers
